steps.premise: Discarded kite string is hard to spot in grass and can wind around a mower spindle.
steps.action: Give the mowing crew time to check for string before each cut.
steps.consequence: The crew can spot string before the mower catches it.
steps.quote: Allow the mowing crew a few minutes before every cut to look for stray kite string. It's easy to miss among the grass blades, where it can wrap around a mower spindle.

steps.premise: Flyers repeatedly launch from one patch and wear it down.
steps.action: Move the launch flags a little each week.
steps.consequence: The worn grass has time to grow back.
steps.quote: Since flyers tend to start from the same worn patch, shift the launch flags a short distance each week to let the grass recover.

steps.premise: Children like to stand directly beneath the kites to watch.
steps.action: Place a bench to one side of the flying area.
steps.consequence: Families can watch comfortably from clear of the kite lines.
steps.quote: Children often want to watch from right underneath the kites. Put a bench off to one side where families can sit comfortably, enjoy the view and stay clear of the lines.

steps.premise: Walkers crossing the grass might run into a taut line they cannot see.
steps.action: Mow a path around the edge of the field.
steps.consequence: Walkers can see where to go to avoid the lines.
steps.quote: Mow a path along the perimeter so walkers have an obvious route across the field. Anyone cutting over the grass could walk straight into a stretched line without seeing it.

steps.premise: A school group can occupy the whole field.
steps.action: List planned group visits on the noticeboard.
steps.consequence: Regular flyers can choose a less crowded time.
steps.quote: Post group visits on the noticeboard so regular flyers can come at a quieter hour, since a single school outing can take up the entire field.

steps.premise: Wind can blow small clips off the work table.
steps.action: Provide a shallow rimmed tray for assembling kites.
steps.consequence: The rim holds the loose fittings together until assembly is complete.
steps.quote: For kite assembly, put a shallow tray with a rim on the work table. The wind often carries off the little clips, and the rim will keep the fittings in one place until the kite is ready.

steps.premise: Quartet members need to decide what equipment to bring.
steps.action: Keep a dated list of the room’s equipment beside the booking form.
steps.consequence: Players can plan what to bring and set up faster.
steps.quote: Keep a dated inventory next to the booking form. If quartet members can see what equipment the room already has, they can work out what to bring and get set up much faster.

steps.premise: A player may arrive after the music has started.
steps.action: Send the door code with the booking message.
steps.consequence: Latecomers can let themselves in while the ensemble plays.
steps.quote: Include the door code in the booking message so anyone arriving after rehearsal has begun can come in without interrupting a piece.

steps.premise: Players may want to mark a bowing as they rehearse.
steps.action: Fit each stand with a groove or clip for a pencil.
steps.consequence: A pencil is within reach when a player needs it.
steps.quote: Give every music stand a groove or clip for a pencil so players always have one to hand when they want to mark a bowing during rehearsal.

steps.premise: Drums can drown out a flute in a small room.
steps.action: Have drum practice pads available for mixed ensembles.
steps.consequence: Players can hear quieter parts while rehearsing a passage.
steps.quote: In a small room the drums can easily overpower a flute. Keep practice pads on hand so a mixed ensemble working through a passage can hear the softer parts.

steps.premise: One ensemble may alter the mixer’s channel levels.
steps.action: Photograph the usual mixer settings.
steps.consequence: The next ensemble can refer to the photo and start sooner.
steps.quote: Take a photo of the usual mixer settings. If one ensemble changes the levels on individual channels, the next can use the photo to get started quickly.

steps.premise: A group is choosing a day to record.
steps.action: Enter the piano tuner’s appointment in the shared calendar.
steps.consequence: The group can arrange to record shortly after the piano is tuned.
steps.quote: Keep the piano tuner's appointment on the shared calendar so a group booking a recording can choose a day just after the tuning.

steps.premise: Some residents seldom visit the shops.
steps.action: Ask residents to tick a box on the signup slip to request home delivery.
steps.consequence: Those residents can receive the bulletin at their door.
steps.quote: Put a small checkbox on the signup slip and ask residents to tick it if they'd like the bulletin delivered to their door. That reaches people who seldom make it to the shops.

steps.premise: The carrier might arrive before a shop opens.
steps.action: Agree with each shopkeeper on a delivery time.
steps.consequence: The carrier can leave the bundle on that visit and avoid carrying it around the route again.
steps.quote: Agree on a delivery time with each shopkeeper so the carrier doesn't arrive before opening and have to take the bundle around the route again.

steps.premise: A reader may move to another home in the neighborhood.
steps.action: Provide a phone number readers can call to report an address change.
steps.consequence: Copies reach the new address and stop piling up at the old one.
steps.quote: Give readers a number to call when they change address. If they move elsewhere in the neighborhood, their copies can follow them and papers won't pile up at the old door.

steps.premise: Shoppers may overlook a bulletin rack among sale leaflets.
steps.action: Place a sign above the rack inviting shoppers to take a free copy.
steps.consequence: Shoppers can spot the bulletin and see that it is free to take.
steps.quote: Even a full rack by the checkout can get lost among the sale leaflets. Put a small sign above it inviting shoppers to take a free bulletin.

steps.premise: A holiday street closure may block the carrier’s route partway around a block.
steps.action: Mark announced closures on that week’s delivery map.
steps.consequence: The carrier can approach the block from the other end.
steps.quote: Mark announced closures on the carrier's map for that week. If a street closes for a holiday and cuts off the route halfway around a block, the carrier can get in from the opposite end.

steps.premise: A household plans to be away for a week.
steps.action: Suspend doorstep delivery for the week the household chooses.
steps.consequence: The household comes back to a clear doorstep.
steps.quote: Let a household name the week it wants doorstep delivery put on hold so it can go away and return to a clear doorstep.

steps.premise: Some children have difficulty gripping a thin puppet stick.
steps.action: Add large loop handles to several puppets.
steps.consequence: Children can move the characters themselves.
steps.quote: Fit a few puppets with large loop handles. Children who struggle to grip a thin stick can then move their own characters without an adult having to do it for them.

steps.premise: Adults’ shoulders can block young spectators’ view.
steps.action: Seat the youngest spectators on floor cushions at the front.
steps.consequence: They can see the full screen.
steps.quote: Lay cushions on the floor in front for the youngest spectators, where they'll have the whole screen in view without adult shoulders in the way.

steps.premise: Sudden darkness troubles some children.
steps.action: Announce the start of the show and dim the lights gradually.
steps.consequence: Those children have time to settle.
steps.quote: Tell the children when the show is about to begin and lower the lights a little at a time. That gives anyone who dislikes sudden darkness a chance to settle.

steps.premise: A wheelchair user needs to operate a puppet from a seated position.
steps.action: Keep one side of the screen accessible and within seated reach.
steps.consequence: The child can perform in the same scene as a standing partner.
steps.quote: Keep the way clear to one side of the screen and make sure a child can reach it from a seated position. A child in a wheelchair can then play a puppet in the same scene as a partner who's standing.

steps.premise: Children operating puppets behind the sheet cannot see the audience’s faces.
steps.action: Have partners exchange sides after each short scene.
steps.consequence: Each partner gets to see the puppetry from the audience’s seats.
steps.quote: From behind the sheet the children can't see the audience's faces. Have partners swap sides after each short scene so both get to see what their work looks like from the seats.

steps.premise: unspecified
steps.action: Put a few translucent colored papers beside the silhouettes for children to test against the light.
steps.consequence: Children can choose a color that shows on the screen.
steps.quote: Beside the silhouettes, set out a small selection of translucent colored paper for children to hold to the light and pick a color that will show up on the screen.

steps.premise: Stacks hide most of the postcard pictures.
steps.action: Display one example of each design upright.
steps.consequence: Visitors can see the options and choose a familiar view.
steps.quote: Stand one card of each design upright. A row of stacks conceals most of the pictures, and seeing them all makes it easier for a visitor to choose a familiar view.

steps.premise: Postage depends on the destination, and a domestic stamp could be issued for an overseas card.
steps.action: Have the stamp volunteer ask the destination before issuing a stamp.
steps.consequence: The writer gets postage appropriate to the destination.
steps.quote: Have the volunteer issuing stamps ask where each card is headed before giving the writer a stamp. The destination determines the postage, and an overseas card could otherwise go out with a domestic stamp.

steps.premise: Some children can tell their story before they can write it down.
steps.action: Have a volunteer write down the child’s dictated message.
steps.consequence: The card carries the child’s own words.
steps.quote: Some children have a whole story to tell before they've learned to write the letters. A volunteer can take dictation so the words on the card are the child's own.

steps.premise: Some visitors arrive late in the day.
steps.action: Reserve a few postcard designs for the afternoon.
steps.consequence: Later visitors still have a choice of pictures.
steps.quote: Set aside a few designs for the afternoon to give people who arrive late a choice of pictures.

steps.premise: unspecified
steps.action: Give writers a short ruler to slide down the blank side after each line.
steps.consequence: One line of writing stays clear of the next.
steps.quote: Provide a short ruler for the blank side of the card. Writers can slide it down a line at a time to keep one line of writing from running into the next.

steps.premise: Cards may be added in the final minutes.
steps.action: Assign a volunteer to take the collection box to the post office at closing.
steps.consequence: Someone takes responsibility for mailing the late additions too.
steps.quote: Choose a volunteer to carry the collection box to the post office at closing so someone is responsible for mailing even the cards slipped in during the last few minutes.

steps.premise: Linens returned on Saturday still have to be washed before Sunday’s booking.
steps.action: Block out drying and folding time on the booking calendar.
steps.consequence: Staff can offer Sunday’s group the quantity they can prepare in time.
steps.quote: When linens come back on Saturday, they still need washing. Reserve time on the booking calendar to dry and fold them so staff offer Sunday's group only what they can have ready.

steps.premise: A caterer might wash the hall’s cloths together with their own.
steps.action: Put a washable hall mark on a corner of each cloth.
steps.consequence: The caterer can identify and separate the hall’s linens.
steps.quote: Mark one corner of each cloth with a washable hall identifier. Then a caterer who finds the hall's linens mixed with their own in one wash can sort them out.

steps.premise: A group’s expected attendance may rise after invitations go out.
steps.action: Set a deadline for the borrower to confirm the number of cloths.
steps.consequence: Staff have time to adjust the order.
steps.quote: A group expecting forty may grow once the invitations go out. Give the borrower a date to confirm how many cloths they need, early enough for staff to revise the order.

steps.premise: A stain might be hidden inside a fold in a clean-looking stack.
steps.action: Open each cloth under bright light before packing it.
steps.consequence: Staff can spot stains and supply a presentable set.
steps.quote: Even a clean-looking stack can conceal a stain in a fold. Unfold every cloth in bright light before packing to ensure the borrower receives a presentable set.

steps.premise: A first-time borrower may find the main hall locked.
steps.action: Include a picture of the collection door in the pickup email.
steps.consequence: The borrower can go straight to the linen room.
steps.quote: Include a photo of the collection door in the pickup email so someone borrowing for the first time can go directly to the linen room even if the main hall is locked.

steps.premise: The group uses tables of different shapes.
steps.action: Bundle the cloths by room and table number.
steps.consequence: The setup crew can carry each bundle straight to its destination.
steps.quote: For a group using tables of several shapes, make up the bundles by room and table number so the setup crew can carry each one directly to its place.

steps.premise: A fountain or a regularly scheduled delivery may mask birdsong at the first stop.
steps.action: Try out the route a few days ahead at the intended walk time.
steps.consequence: The organizer can hear whether noise at that hour drowns out the birds.
steps.quote: Try the route a few days beforehand at the hour you plan to hold the walk. A fountain or a truck making its morning delivery might drown out the birds at your first stop.

steps.premise: A singing bird is concealed by leaves.
steps.action: Point it out with a clock-face direction relative to a landmark the whole group can use.
steps.consequence: unspecified
steps.quote: When a bird is singing from the cover of leaves, give a clock-face direction from a landmark everyone can use, such as “two o'clock from the gate.”

steps.premise: Some walkers need to sit during a long stop.
steps.action: Hold the longest listening session at a bench.
steps.consequence: People who need a seat can participate in the whole discussion.
steps.quote: Plan the longest stretch of listening at a bench so anyone who needs to sit can stay for the entire discussion.

steps.premise: A group may spread out on a narrow path, especially if a walker pauses to listen.
steps.action: Place someone familiar with the route at the back.
steps.consequence: A walker who stops can find the group again.
steps.quote: On a narrow path people can end up quite far apart. Have someone who knows the route bring up the rear so a walker who stops to listen can find the others again.

steps.premise: Walkers disagree on which bird they heard.
steps.action: Write down the song phrase together with the suggested identifications.
steps.consequence: Afterward everyone can compare the same phrase with recordings.
steps.quote: When people disagree about a likely identification, note the song phrase they heard along with the different guesses. After the walk they can all compare that same evidence with recordings.

steps.premise: A chirping phone can sound like another singing bird.
steps.action: Ask walkers to mute their ringtones at listening stops.
steps.consequence: A ringtone will not be mistaken for a bird joining in.
steps.quote: Ask walkers to silence their ringtones at listening stops, since a phone chirping in someone's pocket can sound like a second bird joining the first.

steps.premise: People buying a daily planner pen want to know how it writes on their own pages.
steps.action: Make room for visitors to try a few words in their own planners.
steps.consequence: They can judge how the pen writes on the paper they use.
steps.quote: Make space for people shopping for a daily planner pen to write a few words in their own planners too. They'll want to see how the pen writes on the pages they'll actually use.

steps.premise: A visitor may put a pen down to examine the writing.
steps.action: Set out the pens in shallow grooved trays.
steps.consequence: A pen stays in place instead of rolling to the floor.
steps.quote: Lay the pens out in shallow trays with grooves so a visitor can put one down to look at the writing without the pen rolling to the floor.

steps.premise: The visitor has never used a fountain pen.
steps.action: Before handing it over, demonstrate on scrap paper how the pen writes under its own weight.
steps.consequence: The visitor can begin with light pressure on the nib.
steps.quote: Before handing a fountain pen to a first-time user, show on a scrap how it draws a line under its own weight. They can start writing with a light touch on the nib.

steps.premise: A grip that feels fine for a few loops may tire the hand over longer use.
steps.action: Allow room to write a full paragraph.
steps.consequence: Visitors can judge whether the grip grows tiring as they write.
steps.quote: Give people enough writing space to try a whole paragraph. A couple of simple loops might feel fine even if the grip becomes tiring with longer use.

steps.premise: A left-handed writer prefers the left end of the shared table.
steps.action: Seat that writer at the left end.
steps.consequence: Their elbow has room to move while they write across the line.
steps.quote: If a left-handed writer prefers the left end of a shared table, seat them there so their elbow has room to move as they write across the line.

steps.premise: A visitor wants to feel the extra weight of a cap on the back of a borrowed pen.
steps.action: Identify the pens whose owners allow visitors to put the cap on the back.
steps.consequence: Visitors can try the added weight with those pens and know the owner permits it.
steps.quote: Point out which owners are comfortable having the cap slipped onto the back of their pen. Visitors can feel what the added weight does without having to guess whether a borrowed pen can take it.
